title: Dialogus adversus Pelagianos
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp426.tmp426.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.

passages.original: Nulli enim est dubium, quin Stoicorum et Peripateticorum, hoc est, veteris Academiae ista contentio sit, quod alii eorum asserant πάθη, quas nos perturbationes possumus dicere : aegritudinem, gaudium, spem, timorem eradicari et exstirpari posse de mentibus hominum : alii frangi eas, regi atque moderari, et quasi infrenes equos quibus- dam lupatis coerceri. Quorum sententias et Tullius in Tusculanis disputationibus explicat, et Origenes ecclesiasticae veritati in Stromatibus suis miscere conatur, ut praeteream Manichaeum, Priscillianum, Evagrium Iberitam [Al. Hiboritam et Hyperbori- tam], Jovinianum, et totius pene Syriae haereticos, quos sermone 694 gentili διεστραμμένοςMassa- lianos2, Graece Εΰχίτας vocant;
passages.english: For no one doubts that this is the dispute between the Stoics and the Peripatetics, that is, the Old Academy: that some of them assert that the *pathē*, which we can call "perturbations", namely grief, joy, hope and fear, can be uprooted and extirpated from the minds of men, while others [assert] that they can be broken, ruled and moderated, and restrained like unbridled horses with a kind of jagged bit. Their opinions both Tully sets out in the Tusculan Disputations, and Origen attempts to mix with ecclesiastical truth in his Stromateis, to pass over Manichaeus, Priscillian, Evagrius of Iberia [other readings: Hiborita and Hyperborita], Jovinian, and the heretics of almost the whole of Syria, whom in the native tongue they call *Massalians* (perverted ones), and in Greek *Euchites*;
passages.notes: The Greek διεστραμμένος ("perverted") appears to be a gloss attached to "Massalianos"; the printed text is confused here, and the "2" is a footnote mark. "Evagrius Iberita" is presumably Evagrius Ponticus; the variant readings are given by the edition. *Euchites* means "those who pray".

passages.original: Jovinianus, cujus 2 nunc haeresis suscitatur, Romanam fidem me absente turbavit, tam elinguis et sic sermonis putidi, ut magis misericordia dignus fuerit quam, in- vidia. Illi quoque respondui ut potui. Rufinus non uni urbi, sed orbi blasphemias Origenis et περ\ Αρχών libros, quantum in se fuit, intulit : ita ut Eusebii quoque primum librum Defensionis Origenis sub nomine Pamphili martyris ederet, et quasi ille parum dixisset, novum pro eo volumen evomeret. Num invi- demus ei, quia respondimus, et tanta in eo eloquen- tiae fuere flumina 3 ut me a scribendi atque dictandi studio deterrerent?
passages.english: Jovinian, whose heresy is now being revived, disturbed the Roman faith in my absence, so tongue-tied and of such rotten speech that he deserved pity rather than envy. To him too I replied as well as I could. Rufinus brought the blasphemies of Origen and the books On First Principles, as far as lay in him, not to one city but to the world, so that he even published the first book of Eusebius' Defence of Origen under the name of the martyr Pamphilus, and, as if that man had said too little, he vomited out a new volume in his place. Do we envy him because we replied, and were there such rivers of eloquence in him that they deterred me from the pursuit of writing and dictating?

passages.original: Aut concede mihi aliquem po- tuisse, quod fieri posse contendis : aut si nullus hoc potuit, invitus (??)eneberis, nullum posse, quod possibile jactitas. Inter Diodorum et Chrysip- pum valentissimos dialecticos τερι δυνατου ista contentio est. Diodorus id solum posse fieri dicit, quod aut sit verum, aut verum futurum sit. Et quidquid futurum sit, id fieri necesse esse. Quidquid autem non sit futurum, id fieri non posse. Chrysippus vero et quae non sunt futura. posse fieri dicit : ut frangi hoc margaritum, etiam si id nunquam futurum sit.
passages.english: Either grant me that someone has been able [to do] what you contend can be done, or, if no one has been able to do this, you will be held against your will [to admit] that no one can [do] what you boast is possible. Between Diodorus and Chrysippus, the most powerful dialecticians, there is this dispute about the possible. Diodorus says that only that can happen which either is true or will be true; and that whatever will be, must necessarily happen; but whatever will not be, cannot happen. Chrysippus, however, says that even things which will not be can happen, such as that this pearl can be broken, even if that is never going to happen.

passages.original: Elephanti tantae molis, et gryphes in sua gravitate causentur 4, cur quaternis pedibus incedant, cum muscae, culicesque, et caetera hujusmodi animan- tia sub pennulis senos pedes habeant, et aliqui vermiculi sint, qui tantis pedibus scateant, ut in- numerabiles simul motus nulla acies comprehen- dat. Dicat haec Marcion et omnes haeretici, qui Creatoris operibus illudunt. Vestrum decretum hucusque perveniet, ut dum singula calumniantur, manum injiciant Deo, cur solus Deus sit, cur inviderit creaturis, ut non omnes eadem polleant majestate.
passages.english: Let elephants of such great bulk, and griffins in their heaviness, complain why they walk on four feet, when flies and gnats and other creatures of this kind have six feet beneath their little wings, and there are some little worms that teem with so many feet that no eyesight can take in their countless movements all at once. Let Marcion and all the heretics who mock the works of the Creator say these things. Your doctrine will come to this: that while they find fault with each particular thing, they lay hands on God [and demand] why God alone is God, why he begrudged his creatures, so that not all are strong with the same majesty.
passages.notes: The '4' after causentur is a footnote mark and has been omitted. The shift from 'they' (the heretics) to 'your doctrine' follows the Latin.

passages.original: Aut si justus es, et humilitate simulas peccatorem, mirabimur atque gaudebimus habere te solum et possidere cum sociis, quod nec patriar- charum, nec prophetarum, nec apostolorum quis- piam habuit. Si (Al. sin) autem Origenes omnes rationabiles creaturas dicit non esse perdendas, et diabolo tribuit poenitentiam, quid ad nos, qui et diabolum et satellites ejus omnesque impios et prae- varicatores dicimus perire perpetuo, et Christianos, si in peccato praeventi fuerint 2, salvandos esse post poenas?
passages.english: Or if you are righteous, and in humility pretend to be a sinner, we shall marvel and rejoice that you alone, with your associates, have and possess what none of the patriarchs, prophets or apostles had. But if Origen says that no rational creatures are to be lost, and grants repentance to the devil, what is that to us, who say that the devil and his attendants and all the impious and transgressors perish forever, and that Christians, if they have been overtaken in sin, are to be saved after punishments?

passages.original: genua la- bant, vagitus verba non explicant, balbutiens lin- gua ridetur 3, et aeternae miseriae cruciatus miseris praeparantur. A. Ah! nimium disertus esse coepisti, utnon dicam eloquens, postquam discipuli tui versi sunt in magistros. Antonius orator egregius, in cujus laudibus Tullius pertonat, disertos se ait vi- disse multos, eloquentem adhuc neminem. Noli ergo mihi oratorum et non tuis floribus ludere, per quos solent imperitorum atque puerorum aures decipi, sed simpliciter dic mihi quid sentias. C.
passages.english: their knees totter, their wailing does not form words, their stammering tongue is laughed at, and the torments of eternal misery are prepared for the wretched. A. Ah! You have begun to be too articulate, not to say eloquent, since your disciples have been turned into teachers. Antonius, the outstanding orator, in whose praise Tully thunders, says he had seen many articulate men but no eloquent one yet. So do not play with me with the flowers of orators rather than your own, by which the ears of the unskilled and of boys are usually deceived, but tell me simply what you think. C.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, describing infants.

passages.original: Et quartum nuper ad Hilarium 2 contra doctrinam tuam, multa perversa fingentem. Alios quoque specialiter tuo nomini cudere dicitur, qui necdum in nostras venere manus. Unde supersedendum huic labori censeo, ne dica- tur mihi illud Horatii : « In silvam ne ligna (lib. I, sat. 10). » Aut enim eadem diceremus ex super- fluo : aut si nova voluerimus dicere, a clarissimo ingenio occupata sunt meliora. Hoc unum dicam, ut tandem finiatur oratio, aut novum vos debere symbolum tradere, 806 ut post Patrem et Fi- lium et Spiritum sanctum baptizetis infantes in regnum coelorum, aut si unum et in parvulis et in magnis habetis baptisma, etiam 3 infantes in re- missionem peccatorum baptizandos in similitudi- nem praevaricationis Adam.
passages.english: And a fourth recently to Hilary, against your teaching, who was inventing many perverse things. He is also said to be forging others specifically against your name, which have not yet come into our hands. Hence I think I should refrain from this labour, lest that line of Horace be said to me: "[Do not carry] wood into the forest." For either we would say the same things superfluously, or if we wanted to say new things, the better ones have been taken up by a most illustrious mind. This one thing I will say, so that the speech may at last be ended: either you must hand down a new creed, so that after the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit you baptize infants into the kingdom of heaven, or, if you have one baptism for both little ones and grown-ups, [you must admit that] infants too are to be baptized for the remission of sins, after the likeness of Adam's transgression.
passages.notes: The "he" who writes these books is evidently Augustine (cf. the books to Marcellinus in the preceding context). The Latin "multa perversa fingentem" grammatically describes the doctrine or its holder; the sense is uncertain.
